comparison: Perfect agreement on study population and cohort characteristics (C1, C25-C31, C45-C47). Both evaluations find the cohort design appropriate and well-documented, though peer reviewers note the limitation of single time-point exposure measurement.
Complete agreement on methodological approaches (C41-C44). Both accept the DAG-based covariate selection and pharmacogenetic analysis methods as appropriate without specific concerns.
Full agreement on COVID-19 infection findings (C4, C55, C56). Both confirm that PPI use was not associated with COVID-19 infection after adjustment, with confounding explaining the crude association.
Complete agreement on H2RA comparison value (C6, C73-C75). Both view the head-to-head comparison with H2RA users as a methodological strength that helps address confounding by indication.

Full agreement on attenuated associations in H2RA comparisons (C7, C76-C79, C93). Both accept that pneumonia and COVID-19 outcome associations diminish when compared to H2RA users, suggesting confounding by indication.

Strong agreement on PPI-respiratory infection associations (C2, C53, C54, C68, C71, C89). Both find convincing evidence for associations with influenza and pneumonia, noting robustness across multiple analytical approaches. Peer review also includes C90.

Strong agreement on COVID-19 severity/mortality findings (C5, C59-C61, C69, C72, C91-C92). Both accept the evidence as convincing, though OpenEval notes uncertainty due to wide confidence intervals while peer reviewers express no specific concerns.

Divergent perspectives on baseline differences (C48-C52, C87). OpenEval views these as appropriately documented confounding factors, while peer reviewers express concern about unmeasured confounding and comorbidity severity not captured in the data.

Agreement on propensity score matching robustness (C70-C72). Both view the sensitivity analyses positively, though OpenEval notes the limitation that only measured confounders are controlled while peer reviewers emphasize this as a study strength.

Agreement on pharmacogenetic findings with caution (C63-C67). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to limited power and unexpected patterns, while peer reviewers accept these as part of comprehensive sensitivity analyses without specific critique.

Partial overlap on exposure definitions (C32-C34). OpenEval finds definitions appropriate and clearly operationalized. Peer reviewers accept the definitions but emphasize the weakness of single time-point measurement (C94 also included in peer review).

Agreement on prevalent user design limitation (C95-C96). Both acknowledge this as an important weakness, with OpenEval noting potential null bias and peer reviewers highlighting survivor bias from those stopping due to side effects.
Agreement on selection bias concerns (C98-C99). Both accept the authors' acknowledgment of UK Biobank limitations and collider bias for COVID-19 outcomes as appropriately discussed.

Agreement on protopathic bias discussion (C82-C84, C85). Both accept the authors' arguments against reverse causation using clinical literature. OpenEval explicitly supports the reasoning while peer reviewers implicitly accept it without challenge.

Overlapping mechanistic discussion (C80-C81, C85). OpenEval rates mechanism as UNCERTAIN, noting it's speculative without direct evidence. Peer reviewers don't challenge the mechanistic discussion, focusing instead on methodological issues.

Partial overlap on inappropriate PPI use (C85-C87). OpenEval supports the claim with baseline data showing ~60% lack main indications. Peer reviewers note this in context of confounding concerns about comorbidity severity.

OpenEval provides detailed evaluation of literature review (C8-C24), finding it accurately summarizes prior work and identifies knowledge gaps. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background claims.
OpenEval supports clinical recommendations and context (C88, C100). No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these concluding claims about clinical implications.
